hints: Focus on rate, not yield. Rate of the forward reaction depends on how often reactant particles collide successfully.
Notice that only $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$ are reactants, so the forward rate depends on their concentrations, not on $\text{NH}_3$ or inert gas.
Think about which change squeezes the same moles of $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$ into a smaller volume and how that affects collision frequency.
walkthrough:
**Separate Rate From Equilibrium Position**

This question asks about rate of the forward reaction, not about yield or position of equilibrium. That is a classic trap.

Forward rate $\propto$ collision frequency of $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$

**Recall What Speeds Up Collisions**

For gases, rate increases when reactant concentration or partial pressure increases, or when temperature increases. More particles per unit volume means more frequent successful collisions.

$$\text{rate} = k[\text{N}_2]^m[\text{H}_2]^n$$

**Apply To Pressure By Reducing Volume**

Reducing the total volume at constant temperature squeezes all gases into less space. So $[\text{N}_2]$ and $[\text{H}_2]$ both increase, collisions per second increase, and the forward rate increases. This also increases the backward rate, but the question only asks about forward rate.

options.A: Adding argon at constant total volume does not change the concentrations or partial pressures of $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$. Argon is inert and just adds to total pressure, so collision frequency between reactants is unchanged and forward rate is unchanged.
options.B: Decreasing temperature lowers kinetic energy, so fewer collisions have energy $\ge E_a$. Both forward and backward rates slow down. Students often choose this because low temperature favours the exothermic forward equilibrium yield, but yield is not rate.
options.C: Reducing volume increases total pressure and increases $[\text{N}_2]$ and $[\text{H}_2]$. That gives more frequent reactant collisions per unit time, so the rate of the forward reaction $\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$ increases.
options.D: Removing $\text{NH}_3$ lowers $[\text{NH}_3]$ and slows the backward reaction, which shifts equilibrium to the right. But the forward rate depends on $[\text{N}_2]$ and $[\text{H}_2]$, which are unchanged if volume is the same, so forward rate does not increase.
